Other lower courts reviewing NLRB orders have sought to apply the 
substantial evidence standard articulated in Universal Camera. See, e.g., 
Health Bridge Mgmt., LLC v. NLRB, 902 F.3d 37 (2d Cir. 2018). If any 
generahty can capture the practice, it might be that courts of appeals 
consistently demand reasoned decisions and cast a jaundiced eye on NLRB 
divergence from prior precedent. Mail Contractors of Am. v. NLRB, 514 F.3d 
27 (D.C. Cir. 2008), or failure to consider parts of the record that contradict 
agency findings, .^gregate Indus, v. NLRB, 824 F.3d 1095 (D.C. Cir. 2016), or 
reject an AL J’s determination on factual matters, id. at 1100 (“[W]hen the 
Board reverses an ALJ on factual matters, we examine the disagreement with 
a gimlet eye.”). Conversely, when the NLRB agrees with the ALJ, courts have 
said the Board deserves deference unless its findings are “patently 
insupportable,” Alden Leeds., Inc. v. NLRB, 812 F.3d 159, 165 (D.C. Cir. 2016), 
or “hopelessly incredible [or] self-contradictory,” Raymond Interior Sys. v. 
NLRB, 812 F. 3d 168, 178 (D.C. Cir. 2016).
2. 
Perspectives on Substantial Evidence—Allentown Mack. In 
Allentown Mack Sales & Service, Inc. v. NLRB, 522 U.S. 359 (1998), the new 
owners of a car dealership refused to recognize the bargaining status of the 
union they “inherited,” claiming a good-faith reasonable doubt as to the 
employees’ continuing support of the union. Based on such doubt, the employer 
arranged an independent poll of the employees, who voted 19 to 13 against the 
union. In a subsequent unfair labor practice proceeding, an ALJ concluded that 
the employer lacked the “objective reasonable doubt” about the union’s 
majority status that, under the Board’s interpretation of the statute, would 
have permitted the employer to conduct a poll and to refuse to bargain on the 
poll’s outcome. The Board agreed and ordered the employer to recognize and 
bargain with the union; the D.C. Circuit upheld the order.
On review, the Supreme Court first upheld the Board’s “reasonable doubt” 
standard. The employer had argued that the Board’s policy in this respect 
“irrationally permits employers to poll only when it would be unnecessary and 
legally pointless to do so.” The Court conceded that the Board’s standard “is in 
some respects a puzzling pohcy,” but did “not find it so irrational as to be 
‘arbitrary [or] capricious’ within the meaning of the Administrative Procedure 
Act.”
The Court held, however, that substantial evidence did not support the 
NLRB’s conclusion that the employer “ha[d] not demonstrated that it held a 
reasonable doubt, based on objective considerations, that the Union continued 
to enjoy the support of a majority of the bargaining unit employees.” The Board 
had adopted the ALJ’s finding that six of Allentown’s thirty-two employees had 
made “statements which could be used as objective considerations supporting 
a good-faith reasonable doubt as to continued majority status by the Union.” 
But it ignored other evidence not given weight by the ALJ.
